newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal govt to raise wage offer, deal difficult.
newsitem.headline: Portugal govt to raise wage offer, deal difficult.

text.p: Portugal's Socialist government was ready to improve slightly on a wage offer to public sector employees in talks on Tuesday but officials were not confident that a deal could be done.

In what could be the last attempt at an accord for 1997, the government would raise its proposal from the previous 2.8 percent but would be unlikely to go as high as three percent, an official at one of the ministries involved in the negotiations told Reuters.

"There is a proposal slightly above 2.8 percent, but I have my doubts that it will go as high as three percent," the official said. "It is very difficult for that (three percent) to be reached," he said.
Talks between the government and unions representing the country's some 500,000 public sector employees were due to begin at 1530 GMT with the two sides still wide apart.
Unions have been pushing for significantly higher wage rises, together with a number of other benefits.
But the government, which has staked its credibility on Portugal's qualifying for the European Union's single currency, says that it has very little room for manoeuvre on wages.

Independent economists say that three percent is probably the absolute ceiling for wages if inflation is to continue to decline in 1997, the year when a series of tough tests must be passed for entry to Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) -- monetary union.
The official said that there was a chance that a deal could be done with one of the three union groups, but an accord looked more difficult with the other two which are linked to opposition parties.
The government has not spelled out what it will do if the talks end in deadlock. But the spokesman suggested that the authorities could simply impose the offered increase.
"Logic suggests that this will be the last meeting in order that from January, the new salaries can be paid," the official said.

The Communist-led Common Front union confederation has been demanding at least 4.5 percent to bring the minimum base salary in the public sector into line with the national minimum wage of 54,600 escudos per month.
It has threatened strike action if its demand is not met.
